sections.h2: Where are Duval County property records kept?
sections.html:
The Duval County Clerk of the Circuit Court keeps them in the Official Records, a single series of books that includes deeds, mortgages, judgments, claims of lien, satisfactions, marriage licenses and military discharge certificates. The clerk's office is at 501 West Adams Street, Jacksonville, FL 32202, and the Official Records and Research department sits in Room 1253 of the courthouse.

That department answers at (904) 255-2025. Its hours are Monday through Friday, 8:00 a.m. to 5:00 p.m., except holidays. The recording desk is a separate department, reached at (904) 255-2000 with the same hours.

sections.h2: How far back does the Duval online Official Records search go?
sections.html:
The online portal covers documents recorded since 1988, plus marriage licenses recorded since February 1981. Anything older needs a request to the Official Records and Research staff.

For a pre-1988 document, send as much detail as you have, such as party names and dates, in person to Room 1253 or by mail with a self-addressed stamped envelope. Older deeds for long-held Jacksonville parcels can fall into that earlier set, so start the request well before you need the document at closing.

sections.h2: What does a Duval County copy of a record cost?
sections.html:
Viewing and printing uncertified copies from the portal is free, and paper copies from the office cost $1 per page. Certified copies carry the $2.00 certification fee set by Florida law.

An electronic certified copy ordered online adds a $6 processing fee from the vendor, and cards carry a 3.5% non-refundable service fee. The downloaded file stays available through an email link for 30 days, and you can print it as often as you like. The clerk's general fee schedule lists the lines below.

sections.h2: How do I record a deed in Duval County?
sections.html:
You can record in person, by mail or through an approved e-recording vendor. Every package needs the clerk's Recording Transmittal Sheet attached and completed.

  • Mail-in: send original documents, never copies, with the transmittal sheet and a self-addressed stamped envelope to Attention: Recording Department 1054, 501 West Adams Street.
  • Payment by mail: money order, business check or cashier's check payable to the Duval Clerk of the Circuit Court. Personal checks are not accepted.
  • E-recording: submissions go through a third-party vendor, and the clerk does not endorse any of them.

The clerk processes documents in the order received but cannot promise same-day or next-day recording for mail or e-recorded items. If timing matters for a closing, record in person at the Recording Department.

sections.h2: What recording taxes apply to a Duval County sale?
sections.html:
Deeds in Duval carry documentary stamp tax of 70 cents per $100 of consideration, the rate used everywhere except Miami-Dade. The clerk collects it when the deed is recorded.

Every party to the document is liable under the revenue department's rule, whichever one agrees to pay. Consideration includes money paid, a discharged obligation and any mortgage on the property, assumed or not. A foreclosure certificate of title is taxed on the highest and best bid. Personal representative's deeds under a probated will are listed as not taxable, but the state says there is no exemption for estate planning transfers in general.

Mortgage tax is 35 cents per $100 secured. The statute also sets recording charges of $5.00 for a first page and $4.00 for each added page, with extra per-page modernization and technology charges on top. Ask the recording desk for the all-in figure for your document.

sections.h2: Where do Duval County foreclosure and tax deed sales appear?
sections.html:
The clerk runs both kinds of auction online, through separate foreclosure and tax deed sale sites linked from the clerk's home page. Search results for a street address often tie back to one of those lists.

Under state law a foreclosure final judgment directs the clerk to hold a public sale between 20 and 35 days after judgment unless the plaintiff agrees to a longer wait. Notice runs for two consecutive weeks, the high bidder posts a 5 percent deposit, and objections are due within 10 days of the certificate of sale. Homeowners who are owed money after the sale should check with the clerk within 10 days, because surplus claims must be filed before the funds are reported as unclaimed.

Duval's fee schedule shows the cost side for lenders: filing fees of $401.00 for claims up to $50,000, $906.00 between $50,000 and $250,000 and $1,906.00 at $250,000 or more, plus the $140 plaintiff sale fee and $70 successful bid fee. An owner facing foreclosure who wants to sell instead should talk to the lender and a title company before the sale date.

sections.h2: What should a Duval County seller verify in the records before listing?
sections.html:
Compare the deed on file with the name on the tax roll and your mortgage statements. Small differences in spelling or a missing co-owner can stall a title commitment.

  • Look for any satisfaction not yet recorded after a payoff.
  • Search for claims of lien and judgments recorded in your name.
  • Confirm marriage licenses and name changes recorded in the same index if title was held under a prior name.
  • Run the Property Fraud Alert sign-up so a new filing reaches you at once.

The office charges $2.00 for each year's search, which is small next to a closing delay. Ask the Property Appraiser about homestead status, since the clerk refers those questions out.

sections.h2: How does Duval help owners spot a fake deed?
sections.html:
The clerk offers a free Property Fraud Alert that notifies registered users when a document is recorded in their personal or business name. Scammers record fake deeds to appear as owners and then rent or sell homes that are not theirs.

Vacant houses and inherited homes are the usual targets in a large county like Duval. If you own a rental or an empty property in Jacksonville, sign up before you list it, and recheck the Official Records search whenever a buyer's title company reports something unexpected.

sections.h2: What is a Notice of Domicile in Duval County?
sections.html:
It is a sworn statement that you intend to keep a Florida home as a permanent residence, filed under section 222.17 of the Florida Statutes. The Duval clerk can issue one only for Duval County.

At the Recording Department the fee is $5.00 for the court to issue it and $10.00 to record it, $15.00 in total, and you need acceptable identification. A notarized copy you print yourself costs only the $10.00 recording fee plus the notary's charge. For homestead tax exemption questions, the clerk points owners to the Property Appraiser.

faqs.q: Who is the recorder for Duval County?
faqs.a: The Clerk of the Circuit Court is the official recorder of deeds, mortgages, judgments, liens and other instruments in Duval County. The recording desk is at 501 West Adams Street and answers at (904) 255-2000.

faqs.q: Does the Duval clerk accept personal checks by mail?
faqs.a: No. By mail the clerk takes a money order, business check or cashier's check payable to the Duval Clerk of the Circuit Court.

faqs.q: Which vendors can e-record Duval documents?
faqs.a: Documents go through third-party vendors that the clerk lists, divided into direct submitters for high volume and indirect submitters for lower volume. The clerk says it cannot recommend or endorse any of them.

faqs.q: What does a certified copy cost in Duval County?
faqs.a: The state certification fee is $2.00, and an electronic certified copy bought online adds a $6 vendor processing fee. Cards carry a 3.5% non-refundable service fee.

faqs.q: Can I see Duval records from before 1988 online?
faqs.a: No, the online portal starts with 1988 recordings. Older documents need a request to the Official Records and Research department in Room 1253 or by mail.
